lessons.title: Principles of community development
lessons.html:
What community development is

Community development is a process in which people in a community work together to identify their own needs and act to improve their lives, with outside agencies supporting rather than directing. In agricultural extension and land care, this might be a village organising a grazing association, a women's group starting a seedling nursery, or farm dwellers establishing food gardens.

Core principles

  • Participation – people take part in decisions from the start, not only as labour.
  • Self-reliance and empowerment – build local capacity so the community can continue without outside help.
  • Asset-based approach – start from what the community has (skills, land, water, organisations, culture), not only from what it lacks.
  • Felt needs – work on issues the community itself sees as important.
  • Inclusion and equity – make space for women, youth, the elderly, people with disabilities and the poorest households.
  • Sustainability – environmentally, financially and institutionally.
  • Respect for local structures – traditional authorities, ward committees, churches and existing groups.

Common mistakes

Outsiders arriving with a ready-made project; giving free inputs that create dependency; working only with the most vocal or connected people; ignoring land tenure questions; and leaving when funding ends without building local institutions. Many failed community gardens and abandoned irrigation schemes show these mistakes.

The facilitator's role

The community development practitioner is a facilitator, broker and capacity builder: helping people analyse their situation, linking them to resources (government programmes, NGOs, markets), training office-bearers, and stepping back as local leaders take over.

lessons.title: Participatory techniques
lessons.html:
Getting to know the community

Entry matters. Introduce yourself through the proper channels (traditional council, ward councillor, existing community structures). Explain who you are, what you can and cannot offer, and avoid raising false expectations.

Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA) tools

ToolWhat it shows
Community resource mapDrawn by residents on the ground or paper: homes, fields, grazing, water points, eroded areas, services
Transect walkWalking across the area with residents, noting land use, soils, problems and opportunities
Seasonal calendarRainfall, planting, harvests, labour peaks, food shortages, income and disease by month
Historical timelineKey events: droughts, floods, land claims, projects that worked or failed
Venn (chapati) diagramOrganisations that matter to the community and how close or important they are
Wealth rankingLocal criteria of wealth and poverty, to target support fairly
Problem ranking / pairwise rankingWhich problems are most important to the community

Using the tools well

  • Let community members hold the pen or stick; the facilitator asks open questions.
  • Work in separate groups (e.g. women, men, youth) where needed, then compare results.
  • Use local language and symbols so non-literate people can take part.
  • Cross-check information from different tools and groups (triangulation).
  • Give the results back to the community and keep a copy with them.

Other techniques

  • Community meetings and imbizo-style forums for broad decisions.
  • Focus groups for in-depth discussion.
  • Exchange visits to successful projects elsewhere.
  • Demonstration plots and farmer field schools for learning new practices.

lessons.title: From analysis to action
lessons.html:
Community action planning

  1. Agree on priority problems and opportunities from the PRA.
  2. Set a vision and specific objectives.
  3. Identify actions, using community assets first.
  4. Assign responsibilities and set time frames.
  5. Identify external support needed and who will approach whom.
  6. Agree on simple indicators and how progress will be reported back.

Building institutions

Projects last when there is a strong local organisation: a committee, co-operative, non-profit company or association with a constitution, elected office-bearers, regular meetings, minutes and financial controls. Train office-bearers in their roles, meeting procedures and record keeping. Rotate leadership and include women and youth.

Monitoring and reflection

Use participatory monitoring: the community tracks its own indicators, for example number of households with food gardens, number of livestock dipped, metres of gully treated. Hold regular reflection meetings: what worked, what did not, what next?

Exit strategy

Plan from the start how outside support will reduce over time, and which local structures will take over.

Key points

  • Community development is people-driven; outsiders facilitate.
  • Start from community assets and felt needs, and include marginalised groups.
  • Enter through proper structures and avoid raising false expectations.
  • PRA tools such as resource maps, transect walks and seasonal calendars help people analyse their situation.
  • Build strong local institutions and plan an exit strategy.
